_readme: Routing table for non-plastic materials detected by Stage 0. Each key matches a Stage 0 class name (except 'plastic' which continues to Stage 1). All routes and regulation notes must be verified against current local guidelines before use in a public-facing system. Fields marked VERIFY/CITE need a real source.

metal.label: Metal
metal.description: Aluminium chassis, steel frames, copper heatsinks, zinc die-cast parts.
metal.recyclable_note: Metals are among the most recyclable materials. Aluminium and copper have high scrap value and well-established recovery chains.
hazards: Sharp edges — wear cut-resistant gloves during disassembly
Beryllium copper alloys (rare, found in some connectors) are toxic if machined or ground — VERIFY/CITE
Lead-tin solder on metal chassis joins — wash hands after handling
handling_rules: Separate ferrous (steel) from non-ferrous (aluminium, copper) for better scrap value
Remove plastic brackets and rubber gaskets before sending to smelter
Wear gloves — cut hazard from sheet metal edges
metal.recovery_detail: Send to scrap metal dealer or authorised e-waste facility with metal recovery capability. Aluminium is remelted at ~660°C; copper at ~1085°C. Both are infinitely recyclable without quality loss.
reuse_options: Aluminium heatsinks: resell to electronics repair shops or hobbyists
Copper heat pipes: copper scrap dealer
Steel chassis: ferrous scrap recycler
Intact brackets and standoffs: resell as spare parts
metal.regulation_note: Metal components of e-waste are covered under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. Scrap metal dealers handling e-waste metals must be registered under the Rules. VERIFY/CITE: Rule 16, E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022.

PCB.label: Printed Circuit Board (PCB)
PCB.description: Green, brown, or black boards populated with components — ICs, capacitors, resistors, connectors.
PCB.recyclable: yes — specialist precious metal recovery required
PCB.recyclable_note: PCBs contain gold, silver, palladium, and copper in concentrations far higher than mined ore. They also contain lead, cadmium, mercury, and brominated flame retardants. Do NOT send to general recycling.
hazards: Lead solder — wash hands after handling; do not eat or drink nearby
Cadmium in some older capacitors and semiconductors — toxic if inhaled as dust
Mercury in some older relays and fluorescent backlight inverters
Brominated flame retardants in the FR4 substrate — do not burn
Beryllium oxide in some high-power ceramic capacitors — extremely toxic if ground — VERIFY/CITE
Lithium battery cells soldered onto some boards — short-circuit and fire risk
handling_rules: NEVER burn or melt PCBs — releases dioxins, furans, and heavy metal fumes
Wear nitrile gloves and avoid touching your face
Remove lithium cells before storage or transport
Store in anti-static bags to prevent component damage and reduce dust
Do not use acid leaching at home — hydrometallurgical recovery requires fume hoods and neutralisation
PCB.recovery_detail: Send to an authorised e-waste recycler with precious metal recovery capability. The recycler uses acid leaching (hydrometallurgy) or high-temperature smelting (pyrometallurgy) to recover gold, silver, copper, and palladium. A typical PCB contains 200–500 g of gold per tonne. VERIFY/CITE: actual concentration figures.
reuse_options: Functional boards: test and resell on eBay, OLX, or electronics markets
Individual ICs: desolder and sell (Arduino community, repair shops)
Copper traces: recovered by specialist recyclers
Precious metals: gold fingers on RAM and PCIe slots have highest gold concentration
PCB.regulation_note: PCBs are hazardous e-waste under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 and must be handled by authorised recyclers. Informal dismantling (burning, acid stripping in open air) is illegal and extremely hazardous. VERIFY/CITE: Schedule II (Hazardous Substances), E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022.

glass_screen.label: Glass Screen / Display Panel
glass_screen.description: LCD panels, LED-backlit displays, CRT glass screens, touchscreen glass.
glass_screen.recyclable_note: LCD glass is recyclable but requires specialist processing to separate glass from liquid crystals, polariser films, and ITO coating. CRT glass contains lead and requires specialist lead-glass recyclers.
hazards: CRT glass contains 2–3 kg of lead per unit — treat as hazardous
LCD liquid crystals are toxic if ingested or absorbed through broken skin
CCFL backlights (in pre-LED LCDs) contain mercury — handle as hazardous waste
Broken glass — cut hazard; wear thick gloves and eye protection
CRT implosion risk — never strike or drop a CRT; depressurise safely before disassembly
handling_rules: Never break a CRT — implosion risk and lead dust
If an LCD panel is cracked, seal in a plastic bag to contain liquid crystals
CCFL backlights must be removed by trained technicians and sent to mercury recyclers
Wear thick gloves and safety glasses when handling broken glass
CRT glass must go to a CRT-certified recycler — not general glass recycling
glass_screen.recovery_route: Specialist glass recycling (LCD) or CRT glass recycler (CRT)
glass_screen.recovery_detail: LCD glass: the ITO (indium tin oxide) coating is recovered for indium, a rare metal used in new displays. The glass is then crushed and remelted. CRT glass: lead is extracted and the silica glass reused. VERIFY/CITE: indium recovery rate figures.
reuse_options: Intact working displays: resell or donate
Broken LCD panels: send to specialist recycler — do not attempt DIY disassembly
Intact touchscreen glass (uncracked): harvest for repair parts market
glass_screen.regulation_note: Display panels are listed under consumer electrical and electronic equipment in E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. CRT monitors and TVs are specifically called out due to lead glass. Must be handed to authorised recycler. VERIFY/CITE: Schedule I, Category 3 and 4.

cable_wire.label: Cable / Wire
cable_wire.description: USB cables, power cables, HDMI/VGA cables, ribbon cables, ethernet cables.
cable_wire.recyclable_note: Cables contain copper (high scrap value) inside PVC or PE insulation. Both can be recovered but must be separated.
hazards: PVC insulation contains phthalate plasticisers (endocrine disruptors) — avoid prolonged skin contact with old cables
PVC releases HCl and dioxins if burned — never incinerate
Old cables may contain lead stabilisers in the PVC compound
High-voltage power cables retain charge after disconnection — discharge before handling
handling_rules: Never burn cables to recover copper — illegal and produces toxic gases
Strip PVC insulation mechanically (cable stripper tool) for copper recovery
Discharge any capacitors in the connected device before disconnecting cables
Coil and bundle cables to prevent tangling and physical damage during storage
cable_wire.recovery_detail: Cables are fed into a granulator that shreds them into small pieces, then an air separator or water table separates the copper granules from the PVC/PE insulation. The copper is sold as scrap; the PVC is sent to a specialist PVC recycler. VERIFY/CITE: cable recycling process details.
reuse_options: Working cables: donate, resell, or reuse
USB-A, HDMI, 3.5mm cables: high demand in second-hand electronics market
Copper core: scrap copper dealer (stripped cables fetch higher prices)
Ethernet cable copper: Cat5e/Cat6 cable is a good copper source
cable_wire.regulation_note: Cables and wires are covered under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 as accessories of listed equipment. Open burning of cables for copper recovery is prohibited under both e-waste rules and air pollution control regulations. VERIFY/CITE: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981.

battery.label: Battery
battery.description: Lithium-ion, lithium-polymer, NiMH, NiCd, lead-acid, and button cell batteries from e-waste.
battery.recyclable_note: All battery chemistries are recyclable but none should go into general waste. Lithium batteries are a fire risk if damaged. Lead-acid batteries are highly toxic but have a well-established recycling chain.
hazards: Lithium-ion / lithium-polymer: FIRE AND EXPLOSION risk if punctured, crushed, overcharged, or short-circuited
Swollen/puffed lithium batteries are unstable — handle with extreme care and do not compress
Lead-acid: contains ~30% sulphuric acid — corrosive; lead is highly toxic
NiCd: cadmium is a carcinogen and cumulative toxin
Button cells: mercury (older types) or lithium — toxic if swallowed; keep away from children
All batteries can cause burns if short-circuited
handling_rules: NEVER puncture, crush, or disassemble a lithium battery
Store damaged lithium batteries in a sand-filled metal container outdoors — fire risk
Tape over battery terminals before transport to prevent short circuits
Do not store lithium batteries near flammable materials
Lead-acid: wear acid-resistant gloves and eye protection; neutralise spills with baking soda
If a lithium battery is on fire: use dry sand or a Class D extinguisher — water makes it worse
Swollen batteries: place in a fireproof bag, take to an authorised recycler immediately
battery.recovery_route: Authorised battery recycler — hazardous waste handling
battery.recovery_detail: Lithium-ion: hydrometallurgical process recovers lithium, cobalt, nickel, and manganese. Lead-acid: 95%+ recyclable — lead plates melted and recast, acid neutralised. NiCd: cadmium and nickel recovered by pyrometallurgy. VERIFY/CITE: recovery rates and process details.
reuse_options: Healthy lithium cells (above 80% capacity): test and resell for device repair
Lead-acid batteries: scrap dealer or battery manufacturer take-back (high scrap value)
NiMH AA/AAA cells: rechargeable battery recycling bins (many electronics stores)
Button cells: manufacturer take-back programmes
battery.regulation_note: Batteries are regulated under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 (India), separate from the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022. Producers and importers have EPR obligations. Consumers must return batteries to authorised collection points — never dispose in municipal solid waste. VERIFY/CITE: Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, MoEFCC.
battery.safety_warning: ⚠️ HAZARDOUS ITEM — Batteries require special handling. Do not dispose in general waste. Risk of fire, chemical burns, and toxic exposure if mishandled.

unknown.label: Unknown / Unrecognised
unknown.description: The material could not be identified with sufficient confidence.
unknown.recyclable_note: Cannot determine recyclability without material identification.
hazards: Unknown material — treat as potentially hazardous until identified
handling_rules: Do not burn or incinerate
Retake the photo with better lighting, a plain background, and the item filling most of the frame
If still unidentified, take the item to an authorised e-waste collection centre
unknown.recovery_detail: When material type cannot be determined, the safest option is to hand the item to a trained e-waste handler who can visually inspect and manually sort it.
reuse_options: If the item is still functional, consider donating or reselling before recycling
unknown.regulation_note: Any item suspected to be e-waste should be handled under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 and handed to an authorised PRO or collection point. VERIFY/CITE.
